stem: According to the law of supply, other things being equal, a rise in the price of a good will

options.content: increase the quantity supplied
decrease the quantity supplied
options.rationale: That would be a downward-sloping supply curve.

options.content: shift the supply curve to the left
options.rationale: A price change causes a movement along the curve.

options.content: reduce the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied
options.rationale: The law of supply concerns sellers.

explanation: The law of supply states that quantity supplied rises when price rises.

stem: Which of the following causes a **movement along** the supply curve of maize?

options.content: A rise in the price of maize
A drought that reduces yields
A new tax on fertiliser
options.rationale: A cost change shifts the curve.

options.content: A better type of seed

explanation: Only a change in the price of maize itself moves along its supply curve; the others shift it.

stem: The government introduces a tax of US\$0.20 on each litre of cooking oil sold. The effect on the supply curve is that it

options.content: shifts to the right (downward)
options.rationale: That is the effect of a subsidy.

options.content: does not shift but becomes steeper
options.rationale: A per-unit tax shifts the curve by a constant amount.

options.content: remains unchanged because buyers pay the tax
options.rationale: The tax is a cost for producers, whoever finally bears it.

options.content: shifts to the left (upward)

explanation: An indirect tax raises firms' costs, so supply decreases: the curve shifts left (upward by the amount of the tax).

stem: A government pays a subsidy to producers of maize. This will

options.content: decrease the supply of maize
cause a movement up the supply curve
raise the cost of growing maize
increase the supply of maize

explanation: A subsidy lowers costs of production, so supply increases (shifts right).

stem: A farmer in Masvingo can grow either sunflowers or soya beans on the same land. The price of soya beans rises sharply. What is the likely effect on the supply of sunflowers?

options.content: An increase in supply, as sunflower prices must rise
options.rationale: The price of sunflowers has not changed.

options.content: A decrease in supply, as land is switched to soya beans
An extension of supply along the same curve
options.rationale: No change in the sunflower price has occurred.

options.content: No effect, because the crops are unrelated
options.rationale: They compete for the same land.

explanation: Land moves to the more profitable crop, so the supply of sunflowers decreases (shifts left).
hints: Does the event change the cost of producing or the price of the good?

stem:
The table shows the market supply of tomatoes in a fictional district (illustrative data).

| Price (US\$ per crate) | Quantity supplied (crates per week) |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 8 |
| 3 | 14 |
| 4 | 21 |
| 5 | 28 |

Costs fall so that farms supply 6 more crates at every price. How many crates are supplied at US\$4?

options.rationale: That is the quantity before the shift.
That is the new quantity at US\$5.

explanation: At US\$4 supply was 21 crates; a fall in costs adds 6 at every price: 27 crates.
hints: Compare the quantity at each price before and after.

stem: A severe drought reduces yields on tomato farms in a district. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The supply curve shifts to the right
There is a contraction along the supply curve
options.rationale: The price has not changed first; this is a shift.

options.content: The supply curve shifts to the left
The quantity demanded falls because supply has fallen

explanation: Weather changes production conditions: producers can supply less at every price, so supply decreases (shift left).
hints: Think of the weather and production.

stem: Which of the following explains why the supply curve slopes upward in the short run?

options.content: Consumers buy less at higher prices
Firms always have unused capacity
options.rationale: Rising costs show that capacity is limited.

options.content: Marginal costs rise as output increases
Producers are unaware of price changes

explanation: With at least one factor fixed, extra output requires more costly inputs, so producers need a higher price to supply more.

stem: The supply of a good is Qs = −20 + 10P, where P is the price in US\$ and Qs is in units. The government introduces a tax of US\$1 per unit paid by producers. How many units will be supplied when the price paid by consumers is US\$4?
explanation:
1. Producers receive 4 − 1 = US\$3 per unit.
2. Qs = −20 + 10(3) = **10** units.

Without the tax Qs at US\$4 would be 20; US\$30 is not a quantity.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Producers receive 4 − 1 = US\$3 per unit.
2. Qs = −20 + 10(3) = **10** units.

Without the tax Qs at US\$4 would be 20; US\$30 is not a quantity.
hints: The producer receives the price minus the tax.

stem: A subsidy to producers causes an increase in supply.
explanation: True. A subsidy lowers costs, so producers supply more at every price.

stem: A rise in the price of a good shifts its own supply curve to the right.
explanation: False. A rise in the good's own price causes an extension of supply along the curve.

left.content: A new tax per crate is introduced

right.content: Supply curve shifts to the left
Supply curve shifts to the left
Supply curve shifts to the right

explanation: Own price: movement; costs, taxes and weather: shifts.

explanation: A subsidy lowers costs, so supply increases (shifts right).

stem: What word describes a rise in quantity supplied caused by a rise in the good's own price?
explanation: An extension of supply: a movement along the curve.

stem: Explain why the supply curve slopes upward.

points.description: A higher price increases profit, so producers want to produce more.
In the short run, extra output needs more costly inputs (marginal cost rises).
Producers will supply more only if the higher price covers the higher cost.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A higher price makes production more profitable, so producers want to supply more. In the short run, however, extra output needs more costly inputs, so marginal cost rises and firms will only supply more if the higher price covers the higher cost.

explanation: Profit motive and rising marginal cost.
hints: Link price to profit and cost.

stem: The government of a fictional country raises the tax on fuel used in transport. Analyse the effect on the supply of vegetables sold in a city market.

points.description: Fuel is a cost of transporting vegetables.
The cost of production (delivery) rises.
Supply decreases: the curve shifts to the left.
Producers supply less at each price; the market price may rise.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Fuel is used to transport vegetables to the market, so a tax on fuel raises the costs of supplying them. The supply curve shifts to the left, so less is supplied at every price, and without a change in demand the market price would tend to rise.

explanation: Higher costs decrease supply.
hints: Which curve shifts, and in which direction?

stem:
The government introduces a tax of US\$1 on each crate of tomatoes sold. The table shows market supply before (S1) and after (S2) the tax (illustrative data).

| Price (US\$ per crate) | S1: before the new tax (crates per week) | S2: after the new tax (crates per week) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 9 | 4 |
| 3 | 15 | 9 |
| 4 | 22 | 15 |
| 5 | 30 | 22 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many crates are supplied at a price of US\$3 after the tax?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in quantity supplied at US\$3 caused by the tax, to one decimal place. Include the minus sign.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the tax shifts the supply curve to the left.

points.description: The tax raises the cost of supplying each crate by US\$1.
Producers receive only the price minus US\$1.
So at each market price they supply less (they need US\$1 more for each quantity).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The tax adds US\$1 to the cost of each crate, so producers receive the price minus US\$1. They will supply a given quantity only if the market price is US\$1 higher than before, so at every price they supply less and the supply curve shifts to the left.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Discuss whether the tax is likely to raise the price of tomatoes for consumers.

points.description: Supply decreases; with no change in demand the equilibrium price rises.
The rise depends on how responsive demand and supply are.
Producers may bear some of the tax by receiving less.
A conclusion: price probably rises by less than the US\$1 tax.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Supply decreases, so without a change in demand the equilibrium price rises. But consumers cut back as the price rises, so producers have to absorb part of the tax by accepting a lower price after tax, and the price therefore rises by less than US\$1. How much depends on how responsive buyers and sellers are.

explanation: At US\$3 supply falls from 15 to 9 crates (−40.0%); a tax raises costs and shifts supply left; price rises by less than the tax.
hints: Compare the quantities at each price.

stem:
The table shows data from a fictional farming district (illustrative data).

| Year | Price of maize (US\$ per tonne) | Price of sunflower (US\$ per tonne) | Sunflower grown (thousand tonnes) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Year 1 | 200 | 400 | 60 |
| Year 2 | 260 | 400 | 48 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage rise in the price of maize.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in sunflower grown. Include the minus sign.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the supply of sunflower decreased although its price did not change.

points.description: The price of maize, an alternative crop, rose by 30%.
Maize became more profitable, so farmers switched land to it.
So less sunflower was supplied at the same price: the curve shifted left.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Maize prices rose by 30%, making maize more profitable than sunflower. Farmers moved land from sunflower to maize, so less sunflower was supplied at each price and the supply curve shifted to the left.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **three** other determinants that could shift the supply curve of sunflower.

points.description: Costs of production (for example fertiliser, seed, labour).
Technology or yields (for example better seed).
Weather, taxes or subsidies, or the number of producers.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Costs of production such as fertiliser, improvements in technology such as better seed, and the weather or a subsidy could each shift the supply curve.

explanation: Maize +30%; sunflower −20%; supply of one crop falls when an alternative crop becomes more profitable.
hints: The price of sunflower did not change.

stem: Evaluate whether a subsidy to farmers is the best way to increase the supply of maize.

points.description: A subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right.
It may raise output and lower the price for consumers.
The government pays, so there is an opportunity cost of public money.
Farmers' response depends on weather, inputs and credit.
Better technology, irrigation or roads may increase supply more sustainably.
A subsidy may be inefficient or go to larger farms.
Time lags: planting seasons limit short-run responses.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A subsidy lowers farmers' costs and shifts the supply curve to the right, so more maize is produced and the price to consumers falls. But the government pays for it, so the money is not available for other uses, and subsidies may mainly benefit larger farmers or be inefficiently targeted. The response of output also depends on rainfall, access to seed and credit, and the length of the growing season, so the effect in the short run may be limited. Investment in irrigation, research and roads can raise supply for the long term without continuing payments. A subsidy can help in the short run if well targeted, but other policies may be better for lasting increases in supply.

explanation: Weigh the shift against its cost and alternatives.
hints: Consider the likely size and speed of the effect on supply.
